hero.filename: Taytay Fort, Fort of Santa Isabel, Gates, Palawan, Philippines.jpg
hero.caption: The Taytay Fort, the Fort of Santa Isabel, 1667. It was named in honor of Queen Isabella II of Spain. It was used by the Spanish soldiers as a defensive fort against Muslim raiders. Taytay is a quiet town in the province of Palawan that still bears reminders from Spanish rule. Taytay, Palawan, Philippines.

images.filename: Fuerza de Santa Isabel, Taytay, Palawan.jpg
images.caption: Fuerza de Santa Isabel in the poblacion (village) of Taytay town, northern Palawan, was first constructed as a wood palisade in 1667 under the Augustinian Recollect Fathers. Now, it is one of the most visited tourist destinations in the northern part of the province.
images.alt: Fuerza de Santa Isabel in the poblacion (village) of Taytay town, northern Palawan, was first constructed as a wood palisade in 1667 under the Augustinian Recollect Fathers. Now, it is one of the most visited tourist destinations in the northern part of the province.

images.caption: Carved stone work above the entrance to Santa Isabel Fort. Taytay Fort was built starting in 1667 on the east coast of Palawan facing the Sulu Sea to defend against Moro pirates. Also known as Sulu pirates, they were Muslim outlaws who primarily raided the Spanish. (The Moro people in general opposed the Spanish.) At the time, the site was a massive offshore rock formation, creating logistical challenges such that construction continued until 1738. Coral blocks were held in place with a mortar of lard, egg whites, and lime. Access from the mainland was provided by a wooden bridge, a portion of which could probably be raised at night for added security. In the 19th century the fort was named Santa Isabel Fort (Fuerza de Santa Isabel; Kutang Santa Isabel) in honor of Spain’s Queen Isabela II (ruled 1833 to 1868). Before Spanish colonization, northern Palawan (pronounced ‘puh-LAH-wahn’) was part of the Kingdom of Taytay (pronounced ‘tie-tie’). The town of Taytay was founded by the Spanish in 1623. On Google Earth: Santa Isabel Fort 10°49'42.14"N, 119°31'3.98"E
